summary:
Niğde Province stands under the national framework of Turkey, and no Niğde-specific signal on trans or LGBTI+ legal exposure was identified in the source inventory; the findings below are national and apply in Niğde.

Homosexuality has been decriminalised since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis.

Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised. LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and those receiving an 'unfit report' may face later discrimination in public life.

Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Turkey 47th out of 49 countries. A court case to close Lambda Istanbul was overruled by the Constitutional Court. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association after ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'.

Amnesty International records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but that were ultimately not submitted to parliament. A February 2026 press report of draft legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison was not included in the 12th judicial package, whose passage removed provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible. Whether any such package has since been enacted remains unresolved in the sources.

Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately during a stay.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Turkey 47th out of 49 countries, a regional comparison indicating weaker legal protection than most neighbouring jurisdictions.

The 12th judicial package removed provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, while three draft packages targeting LGBTI people circulated during 2025 without being submitted to parliament. Whether the legislative direction has since shifted is unresolved in the sources.
localsOnly:
Transgender Turkish citizens have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but no comprehensive non-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, and the European Commission's 2025 report found protection insufficient.

LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the Turkish armed forces, whose health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness'; conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and an 'unfit report' may lead to later discrimination in public life.

Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised under Turkish law.

Detainees in Turkish prisons are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and LGBTI+ detainees are subject to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare, with no policy or staff training to identify LGBTI+ needs.

Whether the draft legislative packages targeting LGBTI people reported during 2025 and February 2026 have since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

No Niğde-specific source covers criminalisation, policing, detention, facilities or care access; the assessment rests entirely on national material.
